shows.title: A Bronx Tale The Musical
shows.notes: Changed closing date from Aug 19 (in original Kaggle data) to Aug 5, to match Playbill and Gross Data

manual.context: Reported as close to recouping about 1 month before close (https://www.nytimes.com/2018/06/27/theater/a-bronx-tale-is-closing-on-broadway.html); weekly grosses increased substantially after that announcement.

shows.title: A Gentleman's Guide to Love and Murder

manual.context: Described as a show that "struggled or failed commercially" by the NYT (https://www.nytimes.com/2011/03/24/theater/robin-williams-in-bengal-tiger-at-the-baghdad-zoo.html); Producers were not sure if it would recoup about 1.5 months before closing (https://archive.nytimes.com/artsbeat.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/03/10/american-idiot-to-close/), and weekly grosses were very low after that announcement.   The capitalization was between 8 and 10 million (https://www.nytimes.com/2010/09/28/theater/28billiejoe.html), and we are using the most conservative 8 million in our Estimated Max Weekly Running Cost

On  6/23/2016, the NYT reported that the show would close on 1/1/2017 and expected to recoup before closing (https://www.nytimes.com/2016/06/24/theater/an-american-in-paris-to-close-on-broadway.html).  On 7/26/2016, the NYT reported that the show would close earlier, on 10/9/2016, missing the highly profitable holiday season (https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/28/theater/an-american-in-paris-to-close-earlier-than-expected.html).  Based on the early close, lack of holiday season, and lack of recoupment announcement, it is possible but unlikely that the show recouped.

Even with an extremely modest running costs, would have failed to recoup.  While the exact cap is not reported, we have used $5,000,000 for our Estimated Max Weekly Running Cost calculation, following the NYT estimate https://www.nytimes.com/2012/06/20/theater/fela-and-bring-it-on-go-to-broadway-in-summer.html

In December 2016, roughly 2 months after opening, Crain's New York reported that the show expected to recoup by July 2017 (https://www.crainsnewyork.com/article/20161219/ENTERTAINMENT/161219894/cats-producer-predicts-that-it-will-recoup-by-july).  Its weekly average grosses did not dip substantially after that announcement, and the show closed in December 2017.  Note that using a $4,000,000 capitalization is very likely a substantial underestimate to compute the Max Weekly Running Cost: in 1989 the original production had a roughly $4,000,000 capitalization (https://www.crainsnewyork.com/article/20161219/ENTERTAINMENT/161219894/cats-producer-predicts-that-it-will-recoup-by-july), which is $7.5-8 million adjusting for inflation in July 2016 (https://www.bls.gov/data/inflation_calculator.htm); a 10-12 million dollar capitalization would be more typical, and the Estimated Max Weekly Running Costs would be $643,471 with a $10 million cap.

The Wall Street Journal reported that running costs were higher than a typical musical, and that the needed to be in the "million-dollar club to be comfortable" (https://www.wsj.com/articles/paramour-aims-to-blend-acrobatics-into-broadway-1456787845); weekly grosses were very rarely above $1 million.

Even with an extremely modest capitalization and running costs, would have failed to recoup.  Production had a large orchestra, cast, and ensemble of dancers (https://playbill.com/article/learnin-the-blues-tharps-come-fly-away-will-close-on-broadway-sept-5-com-170449).
Even with an extremely modest capitalization and running costs, would have failed to recoup

shows.title: Elf - The Musical
shows.notes: Merged with a subsequent holiday run, from 2012-11-18 to 2013-01-016.  Closing data manually modified to account for this merge.

manual.context: Variety reports a "reliable estimate" that Elf's running costs are between $500,000 and $600,000, and that the capitalization was "only slightly under the typical $10 million-$12 million mark" (https://variety.com/2010/legit/news/broadway-builds-elf-esteem-1118026584/).  The NYT gives a $9 million capitalization (https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/01/theater/01musical.html/).  With a 9 million capitalization, $500,000 weekly running costs, and a ticketing commission of at least at least 2.67%, the show would have lost money.  Given that these are likely underestimates of the weekly running costs and ticketing commission, the show is unlikely to have recouped.  Note Broadway Grosses are split between https://www.broadwayworld.com/grosses/ELF-THE-MUSICAL (which has the one week of 2010) andhttps://www.broadwayworld.com/grosses/ELF (which has the remaining weeks)

Unlikely to have recouped given grosses, but a small cast (12 including understudies) and a 1991 production was capitalized at only $1 million (https://www.nytimes.com/1992/11/26/theater/the-many-faces-and-facets-of-keeping-falsettos-afloat.html). Could plausibly have recouped with low capitalization and running costs

manual.context: Running costs were estimated to be $300,000 and reported to be "a long way from profit" about 2 months before closing (https://www.nytimes.com/2012/04/19/theater/for-godspell-on-broadway-crowd-sourced-producers.html).

Capitalization reported to be between 8 and 9 million (https://nypost.com/2008/04/02/gypsy-revives-tony-spat/, https://variety.com/2008/legit/news/gypsy-revival-to-close-march-1-1117995801/); we have used the smallest 8 million in our Estimated Max Weekly Running Cost.

shows.title: How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying
Irving Berlin's White Christmas
shows.notes: Merged with a subsequent holiday run, from 2009-11-22 to 2010-01-03.  Closing data manually modified to account for this merge.

manual.context: Producers estimated that it needed to gross $10.5 million during its first holiday season to recoup (https://variety.com/2008/legit/news/white-christmas-hits-broadway-1117996344/).  It grossed $9.3 million, closing much of that gap, but grossed $6.9 million during its second and final holiday run.  It is plausible that it recouped with those additional grosses.  Note Broadway Grosses are split between https://www.broadwayworld.com/grosses/IRVING-BERLIN-S-WHITE-CHRISTMAS (which has the one week of 2010) and https://www.broadwayworld.com/grosses/IRVING-BERLIN-S-WHITE-CHRISTMAS-2008-2009 (which has the remaining weeks)
Even with an extremely modest capitalization and running costs, would have failed to recoup.  An investor in the show is a coauthor of this study, and confirms that it did not recoup.
Even with an modest capitalization and running costs, would have likely failed to recoup (but not impossible if the musical was extremely low budget)

shows.title: Nice Work If You Can Get It

manual.context: In April 2013, a little under two months before close, Hollywood Reported reported that the musical is not expected to recoup (https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/lifestyle/style/nice-work-you-can-get-445898/).  Weekly average grosses from that announcement through close were $659K.  This is substantially below the $834K average of all full-show weeks prior to that announcement, and thus unlikely to change expectations.

shows.title: On a Clear Day You Can See Forever

manual.context: Even with an extremely modest capitalization and running costs, would have failed to recoup
Even with an extremely modest capitalization and running costs, would have failed to recoup

In the show's closing announcement about 3.5 months before closing, the producers indicated that they expected to recoup (https://archive.nytimes.com/artsbeat.blogs.nytimes.com/2010/09/17/promises-promises-will-close-but-questions-remain/).  The show continued through closing, and average grosses stayed strong: the show grossed an average of $1.09 million in full-show weeks up to the announced closure, and these increased to $1.043 million from that announcement through closing.  Given the producer's expectations and the show's sustained revenue, it is plausible that the show recouped.
